howItWorks.intro: The calculator interpolates linearly between a 2020 sea-level baseline and your chosen scenario's 2100 endpoint, then measures the result against your entered elevation to produce a projected rise, a numeric safety margin, and a risk tier.
rules: Rise projection scaled linearly from 2020 baseline to 2100 target
NOAA scenarios: Low (1ft), Intermediate (2ft), High (4ft), Extreme (6.5ft) by 2100
Storm surge adds 3-15+ feet on top of sea level during hurricanes
howItWorks.outro: Scenario choice matters far more than the arithmetic here: the gap between Low and Extreme is nearly sevenfold, driven mostly by how fast the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets respond to warming — a genuinely open scientific question, not a rounding error. Treat every number on this page as a planning range, not a forecast, and check it against your county's FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map and any state or regional coastal resilience study before making elevation, insurance, or purchase decisions.

faq.question: How much sea level rise is actually expected?
faq.answer: NOAA's 2022 interagency scenarios span roughly 1 foot (Low) to 6.5+ feet (Extreme) of global rise by 2100, which tracks the IPCC's broader range of about 0.3 to over 1 meter depending on emissions and how quickly the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets respond. The current global rate is running near 3.6-4 mm per year and has been accelerating since satellite altimetry records began in 1993. Even in a low-emissions future, some further rise is already committed from ocean heat storage and ice already in motion.

faq.question: Why might my actual risk be higher than the calculator shows?
faq.answer: Two things this tool intentionally doesn't model: local land subsidence and tidal range. Parts of the Louisiana Gulf Coast and Chesapeake Bay are sinking 3-6+ mm per year from groundwater withdrawal, sediment compaction, and glacial isostatic adjustment, which stacks on top of global rise to produce relative sea level rise well above the national figures used here. A location with a large tidal range will also see high-tide ('nuisance') flooding show up sooner than a location at the same elevation with a smaller tidal swing, because flooding frequency depends on how often the tidal peak crosses your threshold, not on the mean alone.

faq.question: Does this account for storm surge?
faq.answer: No — this is a baseline mean-sea-level projection only. Storm surge is a separate, short-lived event driven by a storm's wind field and pressure, typically adding 3 to 15+ feet above whatever the baseline sea level happens to be at landfall. The two effects compound over time: as the baseline creeps upward, the same category of storm pushes surge water further inland than it did a generation ago.

faq.question: How precise is the target-year number?
faq.answer: Treat it as a midpoint estimate with a real uncertainty band, not a guarantee. Straight-line interpolation between 2020 and 2100 simplifies a process that's expected to accelerate rather than proceed evenly, particularly if ice-sheet dynamics turn out to be nonlinear — which is one of the largest open questions in the underlying science. A single-year figure here is approximate, not exact.

faq.question: What should I check before making a real decision from this?
faq.answer: Cross-reference the output against your county's FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map, NOAA's regional sea level viewer, and — for a purchase, refinance, or major renovation — a licensed surveyor's elevation certificate. This calculator is meant to build intuition about long-horizon coastal exposure, not to replace the flood-risk documentation used for insurance, financing, or permitting decisions.

howWeCalculate.intro: The projection is a straight-line interpolation between two points on a national scenario curve — not a physical ice-sheet, ocean-dynamics, or regional climate model.
steps: Property elevation is read as feet above today's mean sea level — use a surveyed benchmark or FEMA elevation certificate if you have one, since consumer elevation tools can be off by a foot or more on flat coastal terrain

The selected scenario's 2100 endpoint (1, 2, 4, or 6.5+ feet nationally, per NOAA's 2022 interagency sea level rise report) is set against a 2020 baseline of zero and interpolated forward to your target year
Projected rise at the target year is subtracted from your entered elevation to produce the numeric safety margin

A risk tier is assigned from the size of that margin alone — it does not factor in local subsidence, tidal range, or storm surge, all of which can materially change real-world exposure at a specific address
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: Linear interpolation is a simplification: sea level rise is widely expected to accelerate rather than track a straight line, and ice-sheet contributions in particular are nonlinear and difficult to forecast decades out. Use this as a rough planning signal, and consult NOAA's regional sea level viewer or a local coastal engineer for site-specific figures.

whenToUse.intro: This is a screening tool for long-horizon coastal exposure — useful for building intuition quickly, not a substitute for a site-specific flood study.
scenarios: Sizing up a coastal property purchase and wanting a rough sense of how much elevation buffer remains under different emissions pathways
Comparing two parcels, or two possible building-pad elevations, to see which holds a larger margin by a given decade
Explaining to a co-owner, client, or lender why a modest difference in ground elevation matters over a 30-40 year mortgage or design horizon

sections.title: What This Calculator Actually Projects
sections.body: Global mean sea level has risen roughly 8-9 inches (21-24 cm) since 1900, and the rate of rise has roughly tripled since the early 1990s to about 3.6-4 mm per year today, based on NOAA tide-gauge and satellite altimetry records. This calculator carries that trajectory forward: enter a property elevation above current sea level, pick one of four NOAA-aligned emissions scenarios, and choose a target year, and it interpolates linearly between a 2020 baseline and the scenario's 2100 endpoint to estimate how much rise will have accumulated by that year. It then subtracts the projected rise from your elevation to produce a numeric safety margin and a rough risk tier. This is a planning-order-of-magnitude tool — it is not a substitute for a FEMA flood map, a surveyed elevation certificate, or a coastal engineer's site-specific subsidence study.

sections.title: Global Averages vs. What Happens at Your Address
sections.body: NOAA's four national scenarios — roughly 1 foot (Low), 2 feet (Intermediate), 4 feet (High), and 6.5+ feet (Extreme) of global rise by 2100 — sit inside the IPCC's broader assessed range of about 0.3 to 0.6+ meters under lower-emissions pathways, extending past a meter under high-emissions, high-ice-loss pathways where West Antarctic ice sheet behavior remains genuinely uncertain. But a 'global mean' number is not what shows up at a specific dock or driveway. Land itself moves: parts of Louisiana's Gulf Coast and the Chesapeake Bay are subsiding 3-6+ mm per year from groundwater withdrawal, sediment compaction, and glacial isostatic adjustment, which can add 50-100% on top of the global rate locally. Parts of Alaska and Scandinavia, by contrast, are still rebounding upward from historic ice loss, partially offsetting global rise. Tidal range matters too — a stretch of coast with a 1-foot tidal swing behaves very differently from one with a 6-foot swing at the same nominal elevation, because high-tide ('nuisance') flooding frequency depends on how often the tidal peak crosses a given threshold, not on the mean alone.

sections.title: A Worked Example, and Where Storm Surge Fits In
sections.body: The rise figure here deliberately excludes storm surge, which is a separate, short-duration event driven by a storm's wind field and barometric pressure and can temporarily push water 3 to 15+ feet above whatever the baseline sea level happens to be at the time. The two effects stack over the decades: as the baseline creeps upward, the same category of storm pushes surge water further inland than it did a generation ago. Worked example: a house sits at 6 feet elevation above today's mean sea level on the Texas Gulf Coast. Under the Intermediate scenario (about 2 feet of national rise by 2100), roughly half that rise — call it 1 foot — may be realized by 2060, leaving a 5-foot nominal margin. If that parcel also sits in a basin subsiding around 4 mm per year, add another 0.3-0.4 feet of local relative rise by 2060, trimming the real margin closer to 4.6 feet — before a single storm surge event is factored in. That gap between the national number and the site-specific one is exactly what a FEMA flood map and a local elevation certificate are for.

howToSteps.title: Enter Property Elevation Above Current Sea Level
howToSteps.description: Use feet above today's mean sea level, ideally from a survey, FEMA elevation certificate, or topographic source. This single number carries more weight than any other input, since a foot of error here changes the margin by a full foot.

howToSteps.title: Choose a Climate Scenario
howToSteps.description: Low, Intermediate, High, and Extreme correspond to NOAA's national scenarios (roughly 1, 2, 4, and 6.5+ feet of global rise by 2100). Intermediate is the commonly cited middle-of-the-road planning figure, but High is increasingly the default for critical or long-lived infrastructure.

howToSteps.title: Set a Target Year
howToSteps.description: Pick the year relevant to your decision — a 30-year mortgage horizon, a structure's design life, or a specific planning deadline — since projected rise compounds nonlinearly the further out you look.

howToSteps.title: Run the Calculation
howToSteps.description: The calculator interpolates the chosen scenario's trajectory forward to your target year and compares it against your elevation instantly, entirely in your browser.

howToSteps.title: Read the Margin and Risk Tier Together
howToSteps.description: A shrinking safety margin matters more than the raw rise figure on its own. Remember this number excludes storm surge and local land subsidence, both of which can be added on top of whatever margin the calculator shows.

tips: Source your elevation from a surveyed benchmark or FEMA elevation certificate where possible — consumer GPS and web-based elevation lookups can carry meter-scale error on flat coastal land, which can swamp the signal you're trying to measure.

Run the Intermediate and High scenarios side by side rather than trusting a single number. The spread between them is the actual scientific uncertainty, not a rounding difference you can average away.

If your property sits in a basin known for subsidence — the Gulf Coast, Chesapeake Bay, or parts of the California coast near groundwater-depleted basins — mentally add roughly 20-50% to the projected rise figure to approximate local relative sea level rise.

Remember the projected rise number is a baseline mean, not a flood elevation. High-tide nuisance flooding and storm surge both ride on top of it and drive most near-term risk, even before the long-term mean catches up.
Treat the target-year output as a planning midpoint with real error bars, not a date-certain prediction, and revisit it every few years as NOAA updates its scenario guidance.
